kurz: Why every current account surplus is necessarily a capital export, how 19 cents in the euro exchange rate can move a group's earnings by a third, and who ultimately pays the tariff.

bloecke.md:
Every import is a payment abroad, every export a payment from abroad. The balance of payments records both sides and, by construction, adds up to zero. A surplus on the [[Current account (balance of payments)|current account]] is therefore necessarily a capital export and not money that piles up somewhere. Most debates about trade balances hinge on this relationship. A country that supplies more than it receives acquires claims on foreigners in return, in the form of bonds, company shares, direct investment or bank deposits. The German surplus is therefore matched by German claims on foreign assets, with the associated default and exchange rate risk.

The current account covers considerably more than the trade balance. It combines four sub-balances, and in large economies the last two are by no means small.

bloecke.formel:
Current account = Trade in goods + Services + Primary income + Secondary income

Current account + Capital transfers − Financial account + Errors and omissions = 0

Current account balance = Saving − Investment
bloecke.erklaerung: Primary income is cross-border interest, dividends and labour income. Secondary income is current transfers without anything in return (EU contributions, development aid, remittances from workers to their families). The second line is the balance of payments identity in the internationally standard system. The financial account measures the net acquisition of foreign assets less new liabilities, so that a current account surplus appears there with a positive sign. Errors and omissions absorb measurement errors and regularly amount to tens of billions.
variablen: capital and labour income across the border
current transfers without anything in return
statistical discrepancy, not an economic item
bloecke.beispiel: The third line is not an additional theory. It expresses the same identity in terms of national accounts variables. A country with a current account surplus saves more than it invests domestically. To reduce the surplus, it must therefore either save less or invest more at home. The exchange rate alone cannot achieve this.

bloecke.titel: Composition of the euro area current account surplus
bloecke.unter: Twelve-month total to May 2026. The goods balance alone does not explain the overall balance: services make a substantial contribution, while primary and secondary income together subtract around 171 billion.

bloecke.md: €271.6 billion corresponds to around 1.7% of euro area economic output. The US shows the mirror image. Its current account balance in the first quarter of 2026 alone was minus $212.6 billion, around minus 2.7% of gross domestic product. For 2025 as a whole it was minus 3.8%, after minus 4.1% the year before. These balances are subject to political surveillance. In the EU's macroeconomic imbalance procedure (Regulation (EU) No 1176/2011), the Commission's scoreboard treats a current account balance above plus 6% or below minus 4% of GDP, as a three-year average, as a warning sign. The thresholds are deliberately asymmetric: deficits are considered dangerous sooner because they have to be financed.

zeilen: 2.3bn more than in the previous month

bloecke.md:
Germany is a special case among the large economies. The export ratio, that is, exports of goods and services relative to economic output, has been around 40% for years, compared with the low teens in the US. A slump in demand in China or a tariff imposed in Washington therefore hits the German profit base many times harder than a comparable shock hits the American one. At the same time, the German economy thus depends on a variable that German policy does not control.

July 2026 shows how misleading the balance alone is. At €21.27 billion, the trade surplus was the highest since August 2024. Exports actually fell by 0.8%. The surplus came about because imports slumped by 5.7%. In this way, shrinking foreign trade can look like a success in arithmetical terms.

bloecke.titel: What the trade balance tells you
bloecke.md: A rising trade surplus can have two different causes: sharply rising exports or collapsing imports. In the first case, foreign demand is behind it; in the second, usually weak domestic activity with falling investment, because imports consist to a considerable extent of intermediate goods and machinery. Without looking at the two components, a recession is therefore regularly mistaken for competitiveness. The same applies in reverse to the US deficit, which grows in boom phases.

The exchange rate works on two levels that must be considered separately. The **transaction effect** concerns the real business. A company that sells in dollars and produces in euros earns more when the euro is weak, or can cut its prices and gain market share. The **translation effect** arises purely from currency conversion. A business abroad that is running unchanged appears larger or smaller in the consolidated financial statements in euros, without anything having changed operationally.

The exchange rate does not feed through linearly. Costs in euros are a fixed block that does not shrink with the conversion. This is why earnings always move more than revenue. This leverage appears in quarterly reports as a “currency effect”, where it is often treated as a one-off effect, even though it is structural.

bloecke.titel: Illustrative calculation of revenue and earnings at different exchange rates
bloecke.unter: Model company with $20bn revenue, $12bn local costs and €4bn costs in Europe, indexed to the exchange rate of 1.16 (as of 11 September 2026). Across the range of exchange rates shown, revenue varies by just over a third, earnings by more than a factor of two.

bloecke.md:
The model company generates $20 billion in revenue. Of this, it pays $12 billion in local costs, plus €4 billion for headquarters, development and production in Europe. The earnings contribution in dollars is therefore a constant $8 billion.

- Rate 1.16: 8 / 1.16 = €6.90bn, minus €4bn = €2.90bn earnings on €17.24bn revenue
- Rate 1.00: 8.00 − 4 = €4.00bn earnings on €20.00bn revenue
- Rate 1.35: 5.93 − 4 = €1.93bn earnings on €14.81bn revenue

From 1.16 to 1.35, revenue falls by 14.1%, but earnings by 33.5%. The strength of this leverage depends on the margin. The thinner it is and the larger the cost block in euros, the more strongly the exchange rate feeds through to earnings. A company with a 50% margin loses less from the same exchange rate jump, but still 14.1% of its earnings if all costs are incurred in dollars, and 28.1% if all costs are incurred in euros.

bloecke.titel: Winners and losers from a strong euro
bloecke.unter: The effect depends on where revenue and costs arise relative to each other, not on the industry. The classic exporter at the bottom right is exposed to the full leverage.

felder.text: Sells in euros, buys in dollars. A strong euro lowers purchase prices and widens the margin, a weak one narrows it. Retail and wholesale, parts of the chemical industry, energy processing.
Produces where it sells. Hardly affected operationally, but the consolidated financial statements in euros still fluctuate (pure translation effect without any cash flow).
Revenue and costs in euros. Hardly affected directly, but indirectly through intermediate products, energy prices and the order situation of exporting customers.
Sells in foreign currency, produces in euros. Maximum leverage in both directions, as with the model company above.

bloecke.md:
Tariffs act at the same point as the exchange rate, but they are set politically. The legal basis for trade with non-EU countries is the Union Customs Code (Regulation (EU) No 952/2013) together with the Common Customs Tariff. The EU sets the tariff rates, not Germany. For understanding tariffs, incidence matters, that is, the question of who bears the tariff. Legally, the duty is owed by the customs declarant in the importing country, not by the foreign manufacturer. The empirical literature on the US tariff rounds from 2018 onwards found largely complete pass-through to import prices in the destination country. The exporters therefore hardly cut their prices. A country that introduces tariffs thus initially taxes its own importers and their customers.

In addition, there is the interaction with the exchange rate. If the currency of the tariff-imposing country appreciates, imports in that currency become cheaper and offset part of the tariff. If it depreciates, this amplifies the effect of the tariff. After the announcement of broad US tariffs on 2 April 2025, the opposite of the textbook expectation occurred. The dollar depreciated sharply, and global foreign exchange turnover rose to $9.6 trillion a day in April 2025. A forecast that looks at the effect of tariffs in isolation therefore captures only half of the problem.

A device with a customs value of €10,000 is imported from a non-EU country. The tariff rate is 15%.

- Customs duty: €1,500
- Tax base for import VAT under Section 11 UStG (VAT Act): customs value plus duty, that is, €11,500
- Import VAT at 19% (Section 1(1) no. 4 UStG): €2,185
- Total: €13,685

Without the tariff, it would have been €11,900. The additional burden is €1,785, or 17.85% of the value of the goods, even though the tariff rate is 15%. The reason is that the duty itself is also subject to VAT. For a company entitled to deduct input tax, the burden is lower, because it deducts the import VAT as input tax (Vorsteuer) under Section 15(1) sentence 1 no. 2 UStG. For such a company, only the €1,500 remains as a cost. Private end customers bear the full amount.

The third dependency concerns commodities, and it amplifies the first two. Oil, gas and industrial metals are invoiced in dollars, and Germany imports almost all of its crude oil and natural gas. An oil price shock therefore has a double effect, through the dollar price and through the exchange rate at which this price has to be paid in euros.

September 2026 illustrates this. Between 9 and 15 September 2026, Brent rose from $109.51 to $130.80 per barrel, an increase of 19.4% in four trading days. The trigger was the escalation around Iran. The unusually large gap of around $24 between Brent and the US grade WTI shows that the shock affects the volumes traded by sea, not supply within the US. An American refinery operator and a German chemicals group therefore experience the same world market very differently. Consistent with this, the Baltic Dry Index stood at 3,370 points on 18 September 2026, 53% above the previous year. Copper was at $13,543 per tonne in July 2026, compared with around $6,500 to $7,000 on average in the 2010s.

At the exchange rate of 1.1604 on 11 September 2026, $130.80 per barrel is around €112.7. If the euro stood at 1.06, it would be €123.4. The same barrel would then cost around €11 more, without anything having changed on the oil market. The inflation rate for August 2026 does not yet include the September jump. But even in August, Brent cost just over a third more on a monthly average than a year earlier ($91.08 versus $67.87), with the euro exchange rate barely changed. This explains why German inflation was 2.9% in August 2026, while the core rate excluding energy and food was only 2.4%, and why fuels, at plus 27.7%, tipped the balance.

Two conclusions follow for your own portfolio. First, exchange rate risk arises where a company has its revenue and costs, not where a security is listed. A euro-traded ETF on US equities carries the full dollar risk, while a dollar-listed share of a purely European business carries hardly any currency risk.

Second, the tax treatment in Germany is not uniform. Price gains within a foreign currency security form part of the capital gain under Section 20(4) sentence 1 EStG (Income Tax Act). The purchase and sale prices are each converted into euros at the exchange rate on the day of the transaction, so the currency effect is included in the result and is subject to flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer). A non-interest-bearing foreign currency balance, such as dollars in a settlement account that pays no interest, is by contrast another asset (anderes Wirtschaftsgut) within the meaning of Section 23(1) sentence 1 no. 2 EStG. Gains on it are tax-free after one year. Within the year, they are taxable at the personal tax rate, with an exemption threshold (Freigrenze) of €1,000 per calendar year for all private disposal transactions (private Veräußerungsgeschäfte) combined (Section 23(3) sentence 5 EStG). If the balance earns interest, the tax authorities allocate the currency gain to capital income under Section 20(2) sentence 1 no. 7 EStG, without a holding period (BMF circular of 14 May 2025, para. 131). For larger amounts, it is worth making enquiries.

The balance of payments is based largely on reporting obligations. Under Section 67 of the Foreign Trade and Payments Ordinance (Außenwirtschaftsverordnung, AWV), payments of more than €50,000 to or from non-residents must be reported to the Bundesbank. For companies this is routine; for private individuals it can become relevant for property purchases or larger transfers abroad. The basis is the Foreign Trade and Payments Act (Außenwirtschaftsgesetz), which declares capital movements free in principle and treats restrictions as the exception. One of these exceptions is investment screening under Sections 55 et seq. AWV, which allows the federal government to prohibit buyers from non-EU countries from acquiring stakes in security-relevant companies. This enables the state to block individual capital movements directly. Tariffs, export controls and government transfers abroad affect the current account just as directly. At the same time, the balance of the financial account follows arithmetically from the current account.

mitnehmen: In accounting terms, a current account surplus is identical to a capital export and to an excess of saving over domestic investment. In itself, it implies no value judgement.
A growing trade balance can come from rising exports or from collapsing imports. In July 2026, Germany saw the second case.
The exchange rate affects profit more strongly than revenue, because the cost block in euros does not shrink with the conversion.
Legally, tariffs are paid by the importer. Because of Section 11 UStG, the duty is also subject to import VAT, so a 15% tariff costs the private end customer 17.85%.
Commodities are invoiced in dollars. An oil shock therefore hits the euro area through the price and through the exchange rate at the same time.

begriffe.text: Sum of trade in goods, services, primary income (interest, dividends, labour income across the border) and secondary income (current transfers). It is broader than the trade balance and by definition equal to the difference between saving and domestic investment.

Part of the balance of payments that records the net acquisition of foreign assets less newly incurred liabilities. It is the arithmetical mirror image of the current account. A current account surplus is therefore always also a capital export.

Change in reported revenue and profits caused solely by converting the financial statements of foreign operations into the group currency, without any cash flow or operational change behind it. It is to be distinguished from the transaction effect, which affects real revenue and costs.

VAT on the import of goods from non-EU countries (Section 1(1) no. 4 UStG). Under Section 11 UStG, the tax base is the customs value plus customs duty. Companies entitled to deduct input tax deduct it again under Section 15(1) sentence 1 no. 2 UStG.

Exports of goods and services relative to a country's economic output. In Germany it has been around 40% for years, in the US in the low teens. The ratio shows how strongly foreign demand feeds through to domestic profits.
